# Introducing Kinference: An Open Source Inference Control Plane for vLLM and Kubernetes

November 4, 2026 7 min read

Table of Contents

We’re excited to announce Kinference [kay-inference], a new open source project for building scalable inference platforms with vLLM.

Kinference by Buoyant

We created Kinference at Buoyant after watching our customers struggle to run open weight models in their environments. We designed Kinference to be the control plane layer for the platform you need to build. It uses vLLM to do the underlying inference, and provides the set of features necessary for building an inference platform in practice. This includes token rate limiting, tenant usage and cost tracking, intelligent load balancing, and inference policies.

...

Kinference can be paired with your existing stack. Using Kinference is simply a matter of pointing inference clients to its HTTP endpoint and sending OpenAI or Anthropic-compatible inference traffic there.

Kinference serves a heterogeneous, evolving set of models running on a heterogeneous, evolving pool of GPUs, to a heterogenous, evolving set of clients..

...

In addition to policies and a routing layer, Kinference provides inference-specific load balancing that takes into account signals like GPU queue sizes, historical performance, and the contents of the KV cache on the GPU. This KV-cache awareness, in particular, allows Kinference to send requests to the vLLM worker that will do the least work for that specific request.

Modeling the KV cache content of the GPU can produce dramatic gains in performance for distributed inference. For example, in our public Kinference benchmarks, we showed that, when compared to standard Kubernetes load balancing (labeled “service” below), Kinference (labeled “kinference”) was able to cut median time-to-first-token (TTFT) by 95% and median end-to-end latency by 45% of requests on one workload type.

...

In the capacity benchmark, Kinference served 7.4× the goodput on shared-prefix and about 3.5× the goodput on multiturn. It was able to attain our chosen SLO at concurrency 32 (the highest measured) on our shared-prefix workload, and concurrency 8 on the multiturn workload, whereas the kube-proxy approach was not able to attain the SLO at any concurrency level.

...

Kinference is fully open source under Apache v2. It’s available on GitHub today. Feedback, issues and benchmark reports from other deployments are very welcome.

signals.title: vLLM Delivers Day-0 Support for Kimi K3.1 Pro | vLLM Blog
signals.excerpt:
# vLLM Delivers Day-0 Support for Kimi K3.1 Pro

November 4, 2026 22 min read

Table of Contents

Kimi K3.1 Pro is Moonshot AI's most capable open-weight model: a 2.8T-parameter (104B active) multimodal MoE with a 1M-token context that matches the strongest closed-source models on coding, agentic and knowledge benchmarks.

The main change is attention: K3.1 Pro adds Sparse Attention (DSA) to all 24 full-attention layers for efficiency. vLLM supports it on day 0 on NVIDIA GPUs, AMD GPUs, Google TPUs and Alibaba T-Head Zhenwu PPUs.

## TL;DR

- Sparse attention on a hybrid model: K3.1 Pro keeps K3's KDA + MLA hybrid and adds a DSA indexer to all 24 MLA layers. At long context, a decode step reads about a quarter of the bytes per layer that dense MLA reads.
- One KV cache for three kinds of state: vLLM packs each block's MLA latent, indexer keys and KDA state together. The packed cache runs with FlashInfer and FlashMLA sparse kernels with FP8 or NVFP4 KV and optional MXFP4 index keys, and P/D disaggregation transfers it unchanged.
- Token-sharded prefill attention: up to 1.69× faster time to first token (TTFT) than head-sharded prefill at 340K tokens on 8× GB300.
- Decode context parallelism (DCP) with a sparse indexer: an exact top-k merge with ~10× less traffic makes the attention module 1.3–1.5× faster at DCP8. DCP prefill attention runs 4.1–4.3× faster per layer, and DCP8 holds 7.2× the KV tokens of TP8.
- Fused low-latency decode: the specialized CuTe DSL decode path from Kimi K3 now covers DSA layers, making decode 1.2–1.6× faster on 8× GB300, and 1.9× faster under DCP8.
- Agentic serving: on NVIDIA GB300, up to 375.9 tok/s per user at the latency-sensitive end and 37.8K total tok/s per GPU at the throughput end; on NVIDIA Rubin, up to 815.6 tok/s per user and 68.7K total tok/s per GPU on the SemiAnalysis AgentX benchmark.
- Zero-mismatch RL on day 0: for the first time, day-0 support comes with zero-mismatch RL: vLLM and Megatron produce bit-identical log-probs for both the base model and the LoRA adapter, so the PPO KL is exactly 0 at every step of a 100-step full-model run.

...

| --- | --- |
| Kimi K3, FP8 MLA latent | 13,824 |

...

| Kimi K3.1 Pro, NVFP4 latent + MXFP4 index keys | 10,080 |

The latent and the index keys can be quantized independently. An NVFP4 latent alone already brings K3.1 Pro below K3 with FP8. Opt-in MXFP4 index keys fit 11% more tokens on top and make the indexer 10–20% faster at long context. With both, eight GB300 GPUs hold 1.7× as many tokens as with FP8, and DCP8 multiplies that by seven: about 36 full 1M-token contexts at once, against 3 for TP8 with FP8.

...

At the latency-sensitive end of the frontier, Kimi K3.1 Pro holds 375.9 tokens per second per user. Further along the frontier, it keeps each user above 100 tokens per second while serving 19.2K total tokens per second per GPU. At the throughput end, it reaches 37.8K tokens per second per GPU, about 26× the most interactive point, while each user still sees about 54 tokens per second.

...

### Quantization: Native MXFP4 indexer

The indexer scans the context before selecting 2,048 tokens for attention. MXFP4 reduces each index key from 132 bytes in FP8 to 68 bytes, including scales, cutting index-cache storage by 48.5%. Scoring uses native FP4 matrix instructions with FP32 accumulation and weighted reduction across heads. Keys are reused across query rows during speculative verification to reduce repeated reads.

The smaller index cache leaves more GPU memory available for cached context, benefiting long-context serving at high concurrency. In AgentX sweeps, the MXFP4-indexer configuration delivered 5.3% higher total workload throughput at concurrency 48.

signals.title: Leveling the Playing Field: Building a 100% Offline Kubernetes Docs RAG Exam Assistant with Web AI, Gemma 4, and WebGPU - DEV Community
signals.excerpt:
In this article, we'll walk through the architecture and implementation of Kubernetes WebAI RAG—an open-source, 100% offline Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system running entirely inside the browser using Gemma 4 E2B, EmbeddingGemma, LiteRT-LM, TensorFlow.js, and WebGPU.

...

To transform a general-purpose browser vector search demo into an exam-ready Kubernetes Q&A system, we re-engineered the workflow around a core principle: Prepare once on the maintainer's machine; run identically and offline on every student's browser.

Key architectural upgrades in `kubernetes-webai-rag` include:

- Zero Startup Indexing: Instead of scraping or embedding documents in the student's browser (which would take hours) or importing massive payloads into IndexedDB on page load, the maintainer prebuilds a normalized 16,483-chunk float32 vector matrix (`768` dimensions) alongside a BM25 inverted keyword index.
- Hybrid Search with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF): Combines semantic understanding (`EmbeddingGemma`) with exact Kubernetes terminology matching (`BM25`), grouping by headings and enforcing page diversity.
- Bundled Local Documentation Mirror: Strips external scripts, rewrites links, and mirrors the entire readable Kubernetes documentation snapshot locally so students can verify every `[1]`, `[2]` citation side-by-side.
- On-Device Generation with Gemma 4 E2B & LiteRT-LM: Streams grounded answers and YAML manifests directly from the student's GPU, backed by atomic Origin Private File System (OPFS) model caching.

...

### 1. Concept Retrieval & Real-Time Streaming 

When a student asks a question (e.g., "What is a Pod in Kubernetes and how do I create a Deployment?"), the app:

- Embeds only the question (plus up to 2 recent user questions for follow-up context) on-device using `EmbeddingGemma`.
- Searches all 16,483 prebuilt chunks in milliseconds using WebGPU matrix multiplication and BM25 keyword search.
- Streams a grounded explanation from Gemma 4 E2B with inline citations like `[1]`, `[2]`.

signals.excerpt:
Introducing Physical-Engineering’s Last Exam for agents

November 3, 2026

Authors: Burak Gokturk, VP Research & Development; Rujun Han, Research Scientist; George Lee, Product Manager.

Today, the Google AI & Infrastructure team is announcing Physical-Engineering's Last Exam (PLE), a new benchmark and open competition, developed in collaboration with Mercor, and built to test a frontier model’s ability to complete tasks in mechanical, electrical, civil and structural engineering. 

To help the research community measure and improve how agents handle physical engineering work, we are releasing 29 public tasks, their grading tools, and an open competition leaderboard at ple-bench.com.

...

### Inside PLE: Real-world tasks built with practicing engineers

PLE closes this evaluation gap with 85 long-horizon tasks across four core disciplines: mechanical (30 tasks), electrical (27 tasks), civil (18 tasks), and structural (10 tasks) engineering.

Close this modal

Instead of answering a single prompt, an agent works inside a containerized project folder — built on Mercor’s Archipelago environment — that mirrors what a practicing engineer receives on the job. Each task holds an average of 61 files (5,170 total files across the benchmark), including PDFs, spreadsheets, emails, 2D CAD drawings, 3D BIM models, and document revisions. The agent must reason through these files, find the governing building codes and physical limits, run calculations, and generate production-ready deliverables that a licensed reviewer would review and approve.

...

### All frontier models score below 50%

We tested 14 frontier models on PLE using seven publicly available agent harnesses (Antigravity, Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, OpenCode, OpenHands, and Pi). Because PLE evaluates both code compliance and cost efficiency, agents only earn points if their design passes every hard safety check first. Our baseline results show a wide gap between current models and real-world engineering requirements:

- High headroom: All frontier models score below 50% on our private test set, with the highest-performing model on its native harness reaching a mean score of 48.3%.
- Hard safety gates: While the top-scoring agent configuration satisfied 91% of individual constraints on co-authored tasks, only 41.3% of its deliverables passed every hard safety and feasibility check required.
- Model vs. harness impact: Choice of model drives performance far more than the harness (up to a 50-point spread across models, versus a median 3-point spread across harnesses for the same model), though harnesses significantly affect run cost.

signals.title: Kimi K3.1 Pro on AMD Instinct GPUs
signals.excerpt:
# Kimi K3.1 Pro on AMD Instinct GPUs: Day-0 support and optimization

 Nov 04, 2026

# TL;DR

- Kimi K3.1 Pro, Moonshot AI’s open-weight, natively multimodal agentic model (2.8T total and 104B activated parameters, 1M-token context), serves on 8× AMD Instinct™ MI355X GPUs with both ATOM and vLLM on day 0, from the released MXFP4 checkpoint and with its DSpark speculative-decoding draft.
- K3.1 Pro keeps Kimi K3’s hybrid architecture: 69 Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) layers and 24 latent-attention layers over an 896-expert MXFP4 MoE. It adds a sparse indexer (DSA) to every one of the 24 attention layers, which selects 2,048 tokens of history per query. ATOM serves the indexed layers on its shared DSA path, with an FP8 index cache next to the FP8 latent KV cache
- ATOM: native KDA and sparse MLA kernels, the routed experts on FlyDSL’s MXFP4 grouped MoE, per-channel FP8 attention applied at start-up, and a DSpark draft that shares the target’s KV cache and runs as a captured CUDA graph.
- vLLM: memory-efficient sparse attention with decode context parallelism (DCP) for long-context serving, alongside a specialized decode path for low-latency interactive workloads
- Accuracy on Moonshot AI’s Kimi Vendor Verifier, at reasoning effort max: OCRBench 0.871 (Moonshot reference 0.872); tool-call JSON schema 0.991.

...

Kimi K3.1 Pro runs on AMD Instinct MI350 Series GPUs from day 0 with ATOM, the AMD inference engine, on ROCm™ software with AITER and FlyDSL kernels. The model is post-trained from Kimi K3 with large-scale joint reinforcement learning. Moonshot AI describes it as its most capable 3T-class model, with a 1M-token context window, selectable reasoning effort (low, high, max), native tool calling and image input.

...

- Hybrid attention, now sparse: Of the 93 decoder layers, 69 use Kimi Delta Attention, a gated linear attention with a fixed-size recurrent state per request. The other 24 are gated latent attention (MLA) layers: every fourth layer, plus the last. In K3.1 Pro each of them also has an indexer (32 heads of dimension 128) that scores the request’s history and selects the top 2,048 tokens for attention. Attention then reads at most 2,048 tokens per query however long the context grows; only the lightweight indexer scores the whole history.
- Two small caches per attention layer: Each MLA layer caches one 576-wide latent per token (512 compressed KV plus 64 RoPE dimensions) and one index key per token.
- A wide, latent MoE: There are 896 routed experts, 16 active per token, plus two shared experts. The routed experts work in a 3,584-wide latent space, half the 7,168-wide hidden size, and use the SiTU-GLU activation. Only the first layer is dense.
- MXFP4, quantization-aware trained: The routed experts are stored in MXFP4 (one E8M0 scale per 32 values). Attention, the indexer, the shared experts, the dense MLP, the latent up/down projections, the router, the LM head and the vision encoder are BF16.
- DSpark speculative decoding: A separate five-layer MLA draft reads hidden states from five of the target’s last layers and proposes a block of draft tokens per step.

...

# Serving with ATOM

ATOM serves Kimi K3.1 Pro with tensor parallelism over the eight GPUs of one MI355X node, for text and image input, from the released MXFP4 checkpoint without conversion. With the DSpark draft loaded, each GPU peaks at about 199 GB of its 288 GB during start-up, and a single 1M-token request fits on one node.

...

PTPC FP8 attention: At start-up, ATOM re-quantizes the BF16 attention and dense linears to FP8 with one scale per output channel, with activations scaled per token at run time (--online_quant_config with ptpc_fp8): 559 linears per rank, done in about 2 seconds. The routed experts, the KDA convolutions, the vision encoder and the indexer-packed down-projection keep their stored formats.

DSpark speculative decoding: The draft’s 576-wide latent has the same shape as the target’s MLA layers, so ATOM binds the five draft layers into the target’s KV pool as extra rows, and they inherit the FP8 cache dtype. The draft block, which proposes all draft tokens in one parallel pass, is captured in a CUDA graph.

...

vLLM supports Kimi K3.1 Pro on AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs with the MXFP4 checkpoint and DSpark speculative decoding. Built on AITER and FlyDSL kernels, the ROCm implementation combines memory-efficient sparse attention with decode context parallelism (DCP) for long-context serving, alongside a specialized decode path for low-latency interactive workloads.

# Building Private Offline RAG in Pure Python: Ollama, SQLite-Vec & Function Calling Agents
Paying metered per-million-token bills to OpenAI or Anthropic is killing AI startup margins in 2026. If your application handles 10,000 queries per day with multi-turn context and reasoning models, you are bleeding between $800 and $3,000 every single month in variable API costs. Furthermore, healthcare, legal, and enterprise clients flatly refuse to allow sensitive internal documents to cross public cloud network boundaries.
In this deep architectural breakdown, we will build a **100% private, zero-cloud RAG pipeline and autonomous agent engine in pure Python**. It runs entirely on local hardware, costs $0.00 in ongoing API subscription fees, and operates with sub-millisecond local vector retrieval.

Here is the operational pipeline:
```
[User Query / Document Input]

              ↓

  [Top-K Semantic Context Assembly + Prompt Guardrails]

signals.excerpt:
# Together Compiler: Continual Compilation for AI inference

- Authors Reyna Abhyankar, Dylan Lim, and Simran Arora
- Table of contents 40+ Models Chosen for Production...40+ Models Chosen for Production...40+ Models Chosen for Production...
- Links in this article Polymorphic Inference Paper

...

### We introduce Together Compiler (TKCC), the first truly continual RSI system that leverages high-throughput agents to optimize to diverse inference workloads.

In less than 24 hours, TKCC achieves up to 2.6x higher TPS across frontier open source models (Kimi K3, GLM 5.3, MiniMax M3.1-Flash, DeepSeek v4.1-Flash), sets the state-of-the-art on SemiAnalysis’ InferenceX benchmark for low-latency with 1111 TPS on MiniMax M3.1-Flash and 1205 TPS on DeepSeek v4.1-Flash, and outperforms available open-source megakernels by 1.7x on their workhorse Llama 1B batch size 1 setting. Furthermore, TKCC generalizes to domains beyond language model inference (weather modeling, PDE, time-series, and biology). This performance boost is enabled by TKCC’s 252x higher experiment throughput compared to baseline agentic RSI performance optimization systems. Together Compiler is serving trillions of tokens today.

...

TKCC takes as input the traffic shape, model, and hardware. TKCC uses agents to generate a series of optimizations for an inference engine.

...

1. TKCC maximizes experimentation throughput and minimizes GPU idle time during agent optimization

‍ Most existing agentic inference optimization systems require agents to launch and teardown engines like VLLM, SGLang, or TRT-LLM to test each new experiment. However, engine start times are tens of minutes, significantly impeding experimentation throughput (see table below). Instead, TKCC proposes a new paradigm of “persistent engines” where the engine starts up once and can hot-reload any candidate forward pass, without any restarts. To ensure that the persistent engines constantly have new optimizations to test, TKCC spawns multiple agents that continually generate ideas and communicate via a message board to parallelize their efforts.

signals.excerpt:
# Together AI Releases Together Compiler: Agents Make Inference Up to 2.6x Faster

By

Asif Razzaq

November 5, 2026

Together AI has introduced Together Compiler (TKCC), an agent-driven system that keeps re-optimizing inference as production traffic changes. Together Compiler already runs on several of Together’s serverless endpoints. The core claim for developers: an engine tuned once goes stale, so tuning should never stop.

## TL;DR

- System: It is an optimization system, tested on Kimi K3, GLM 5.3, MiniMax M3.1 Flash, DeepSeek v4.1 Flash and Llama 1B.
- Runs on: NVIDIA B200, B300, GB300, H100, AMD MI355X and AWS Trainium2. Each run used at most 2 nodes per model.
- Performance: Up to 2.6x higher TPS than the best published InferenceX configurations, in under 24 hours per setting.
- Best: 1,111 P90 TPS per user on MiniMax M3.1 Flash (B200, batch size 1), 1.8x over the 633 TPS baseline.
- Worst: GLM 5.3 on MI355X moved only from 463 to 480 TPS (about 4%).

...

Together Compiler is a continual compilation loop from Together AI that uses coding agents to rewrite a model’s forward pass. It takes a server launch command, a traffic profile and a hardware configuration. Agents propose faster forward passes, and a persistent engine measures each one. The winning code ships into the serving engine. When traffic drifts, the loop runs again.

...

## Benchmarks: how fast is Together Compiler?

On SemiAnalysis InferenceX‘s AgentX workload, Together Compiler beat the best open configurations by up to 2.6x TPS. Each setting ran under 24 hours on at most 2 nodes.

Batch size 1, P90 TPS per user (Together Compiler vs InferenceX best, self-reported):

- MiniMax M3.1 Flash (B200): 1,111 vs 633
- DeepSeek v4.1 Flash (GB300): 1,205 vs 943
- GLM 5.3 (B200): 417 vs 329
- Kimi K3 (GB300): 450 vs 423
- GLM 5.3 (MI355X): 480 vs 463

For MiniMax, the cost model picked TP8 over the baseline’s TP4. That halves each GPU’s weight traffic in memory-bound decode.

signals.title: Cohere Brings Embed 5 and Rerank 5 to OpenRouter’s Unified API – Unite.AI
signals.excerpt:
Cohere announced on November 4, 2026 that its Embed 5 and Rerank 5 retrieval models are available on OpenRouter. Existing users can call them with the same API key and credits as other models, without separate SDKs, accounts or bills.

The models cover the retrieval stages of a retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, pipeline: Embed 5 converts documents and queries into vectors, Rerank 5 rescores candidates against the query, and any chat model on OpenRouter can generate the final answer. Cohere also published a Python reference workflow spanning indexing, retrieval, relevance filtering and cited generation.

...

The OpenRouter rollout expands distribution rather than introducing another model generation. Cohere introduced Embed 5 on September 30, 2026, and Rerank 5 on October 21, 2026; both families offer Pro and Fast tiers.

...

The reference pipeline retrieves 20 chunks by cosine similarity, sends them with the question to Rerank 5, keeps as many as five results and discards scores below a demonstration threshold of 0.3. Reranking reads the query and each candidate together rather than relying only on vector proximity, and can operate after semantic, keyword or hybrid search without Embed 5.

Cohere says Rerank 5’s calibrated scores remain consistent across queries and domains, allowing one threshold to decide which context reaches a generator; its launch documentation describes a score of 0.7 as a 70% probability that a document is useful. Pro is intended for reasoning-heavy queries and long or domain-specific documents, while Fast targets high-volume search and agents that search repeatedly. The models support a 32K-token context and can process JSON records or tables formatted as YAML strings.

...

The sample requires Python 3.10 or newer, an OpenRouter API key and Python SDK, and NumPy for its in-memory vector store. Production implementations are directed to replace that store with a vector database. OpenRouter’s RAG guidance presents reranking as a precision-versus-latency choice: it can improve results when a broad candidate set must be narrowed, but adds an API call and is less suitable when minimum latency is the priority.

signals.excerpt:
NVIDIA said three software optimizations raised decode throughput for Ant Group inclusionAI’s Ling-3.0-flash model by 42.5% on a single DGX Spark desktop system.

Tests across all 1,319 GSM8K questions increased throughput to 53.89 tokens per second from 37.81 tokens per second, while accuracy changed to 96.82% from 96.89%, a statistically undetectable difference, NVIDIA said.

The test used Ling-3.0-flash-fp4, a mixture-of-experts model with 124 billion total parameters and 5.1 billion active parameters per token. The model has a native 256,000-token context window.

DGX Spark uses NVIDIA’s GB10 Grace Blackwell Superchip and has 128 GB of unified memory and 273 GB/s of memory bandwidth. NVIDIA rates the system for inference on models with as many as 200 billion parameters and says it can deliver up to 1 petaFLOP of sparse FP4 computing performance.

NVIDIA profiled the model at batch size one and found decoding was constrained by memory reads, particularly in mixture-of-experts computation and the language-model output head. The baseline followed the official W4A8 recipe, using FlashInfer MXFP4 MoE kernels, CUTLASS dense GEMM and an FP32 language-model head.

...

The first change replaced FlashInfer’s MoE backend with Humming, an independent kernel library that compiles kernels at runtime for specific matrix shapes, data types and GPUs. NVIDIA said the change supported the model’s narrow 768-wide expert layer and increased throughput by 9.3% to 39.45 tokens per second.

The second change applied FP8 quantization to the language-model head at load time. The head is a 157,184-by-2,560 BF16 matrix, and NVIDIA said FP8 halves the memory reads required for that layer. Humming combined with the FP8 head reached 43.94 tokens per second, up 21.7% from baseline.

The third change used multi-token prediction speculative decoding through Ling-3.0-flash’s built-in NEXTN prediction layer, eliminating the need for a separate draft model. On the synthetic test, 3.90 tokens were accepted per round and throughput rose to 102.88 tokens per second, a 185.1% increase from baseline.

...

With all three changes enabled on GSM8K, time per output token fell to 18.56 milliseconds from 26.45 milliseconds. Mean latency declined 24.5% to 11.49 seconds from 15.21 seconds.

signals.title: Google Launches LiteRT Tensor API for Building, Customizing, and Optimizing ML Models for On-Device - InfoQ
signals.excerpt:
Google has introduced the LiteRT Tensor API, a lightweight C++ API that allows developers to build, customize, and optimize machine learning models directly for on-device execution. According to Google, it combines the flexibility of native model authoring with cross-platform portability.

...

The LiteRT Tensor API aims to address these challenges by allowing developers to build computation graphs operation by operation in C++. This provided greater control over model architecture, optimization, and accelerator execution, while enabling the same graphs to run through LiteRT on CPU, GPU, and NPU hardware without requiring a rewrite for each new target.

Beyond providing full control over model graphs, other key capabilities of the API include direct weight ingestion, allowing developers to load weights directly from checkpoints, including Hugging Face `.safetensors` files; zero-copy buffer interoperability, which avoids copying accelerator buffers across pre-processing, inference, and post-processing; and compatibility with AI coding agents, which can construct, modify, validate, and benchmark model graphs by generating C++ code.

...

> We ran the same C++ code for the SAM 2 model on the GPUs of three devices: a macOS laptop (Metal), an iOS phone (Metal), and an Android phone (OpenCL). In our tests on the MacBook Pro, it ran about 1.5x faster than Apple MLX (fp16, image encoder plus mask decoder).

Google emphasized the fact that the coding agent could make a number of optimizations thanks to the model graph being defined in plain C++. Specifically, it "moved SAM 2's per-frame decisions, such as whether the object is still visible, from CPU code into the graph" and rewrote operations that triggered CPU fallback on WebGPU using GPU-compatible arithmetics.

...

signals.title: Build a RAG Pipeline With Evals: 12 Steps, 90 Min [2026]
signals.excerpt:
# Build a RAG Pipeline With Evals: 12 Steps, 90 Min [2026]

Tom Vance Updated Nov 2, 2026 · 36 min read

Mistral released the Large 4 weights on October 29, 2026, three weeks after the October 6 API preview, and DeepSeek has served V4.1-Flash on its API since September 10. Both models offer a 1-million-token context window. That number tempts teams to skip retrieval and paste whole manuals into every prompt. A RAG pipeline still wins on cost, latency, freshness and the one question auditors ask first: which document produced this sentence?

The project below is a small Python package called `ragkit`. It chunks documents by heading, searches them with dense vectors and BM25 keywords at the same time, fuses the two rankings, and asks an LLM for an answer with numbered citations. A harness then scores retrieval hits, answer correctness, faithfulness and resistance to prompt injection. Twelve steps and roughly 90 minutes get you there.

...

## What the Finished RAG Pipeline Does and Which Models Plug In

A question enters the system and takes five hops. The retriever pulls 30 dense candidates and 30 keyword candidates, fuses them into one ranking, and keeps the top six chunks. The prompt builder wraps each chunk in a labeled block and tells the model that the blocks are untrusted data. The model answers with bracketed citations such as [2], or says it does not know. The CLI prints the answer, the sources and the cost in dollars.

signals.title: Introducing AgentEnv: An Open-Source Framework for Building RL Environments | Scale Labs
signals.excerpt:
10/5/2026

# Introducing AgentEnv: An Open-Source Framework for Building RL Environments

By Edgar Arakelyan, Tejas Polakam, Yzabelle Go

An agent is only as good as the world it operates in, and building worlds that are realistic, accurate, and scalable all at once is the hard part of scaling RL. Every RL environment Scale builds runs on AgentEnv. Today we're open-sourcing it.

...

Most tools for agent training start from the task and build a world around it. AgentEnv’s philosophy starts from the world first, so one Environment can host many Tasks and many agents. AgentEnv is built on two core principles

Building blocks: What an Environment is made of. An Environment is built from versioned composable blocks: Environments like Slack or Gmail, an Artifact of data that populates them, and Rules (the clock, triggers, and roles) that govern how it behaves.

Interoperability: What an Environment works with. An Environment doesn't assume anything about who or what runs it. Any agent can connect to it, any sandbox can host it, and your cloud can run it, all through open protocols instead of custom glue.

...

#### Designed for Interoperability

Agent Agnostic. An Environment's card tells an agent which tools it serves and how to reach them, over MCP, REST or a generated CLI. An agent's Agent Card, from the open A2A protocol, does the same in the other direction.

Pair any Environment Card with any Agent Card and the agent can start work, with no custom wiring. The same Task runs unchanged and consistent on Claude Code, OpenAI's agents, or any of your own custom agents.

...

A Task is constructed as a DAG of AgentEnv steps. Each step represents a primitive action on an Agent, the Environment and more, like setting up the world, loading data, setting the clock, bringing in an agent, handing it the work, collecting what it made, grading the result with a rubric or a strict check.

...

### What comes out of the box

AgentEnv ships 48 built-in step types, covering everything from deploying an Environment to setting its Rules of the World to grading trajectories. Most RL Tasks can be built from these alone, with no new code. For the rest, you can add your own steps as plugins.

signals.title: Baidu Open-Sources 280-Billion-Parameter ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base, Setting New SOTA on Multiple Benchmarks for Same-Size Models
signals.excerpt:
# Baidu Open-Sources 280-Billion-Parameter ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base, Setting New SOTA on Multiple Benchmarks for Same-Size Models

Time : Nov 5, 2026 Read : 3 minute

On November 5, Baidu officially open-sourced its new base model, ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base. It set new SOTA results among models of the same size on multiple benchmarks spanning knowledge, reasoning, math, code, multilingual, and long-context tasks, outperforming comparable models such as DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base and Hy3-preview-Base.

The model uses an MoE architecture, with 280 billion total parameters and 14 billion activated parameters. It was pretrained on 33.5 trillion tokens, with a pretraining context length of up to 128K, and supports a context length of up to 1 million tokens during fine-tuning and inference.

With efficiency as the main focus, ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base introduces several algorithmic innovations at the system level. In its attention mechanism, it introduces Latent-Gated Sparse Attention, combining HCA and MLA to compress historical information and provide fine-grained access to historical positions. It uses low-rank gated attention to reduce the number of gating projection weight parameters by 75%, while enhancing expressiveness through virtual head attention.

For expert routing, it adopts Multi-Router Latent MoE, using multiple independent routers to improve expert selection effectiveness. For the training objective, it introduces ECHO, which reuses the last layer of the backbone to learn to predict subsequent tokens and removes the need for an extra MTP module. On the large-model infrastructure side, it optimizes the distributed Muon optimizer and introduces the FlashMask-4 attention operator, further improving communication and memory utilization efficiency in large-scale training.

Competition among large models is now evolving toward coordinated progress in model capabilities, training efficiency, and use-case innovation. The open-sourcing of ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base lowers the barrier to specialized model development while providing developers with an efficient technical foundation for building customized specialized models.

signals.excerpt:
# Kakao Releases Two Kanana-2-embedding Models, Core Technology for Personalized AI Agents, as Open Source

Photo - Kakao

Kakao said it has released two Kanana-2-embedding models, the underlying technology for personalized AI agents, as open source on Hugging Face.

The two models are Kanana-2-3b-embedding, with 3 billion parameters, and Kanana-2-1.3b-embedding, with 1.3 billion parameters. The release follows four Kanana small language models (SLMs) that Kakao open-sourced in July. Kakao has built on its own language models to advance its embedding technology, improving search performance and efficiency across a range of services.

An embedding model expresses the meaning of text as numbers and finds information relevant to a user's question. A general language model understands the question and generates an answer, while an embedding model finds the information the answer needs based on the semantic similarity between the question and the information. Users can search for information with a similar meaning even when they cannot remember the exact words.

This technology plays an important role in enabling personalized AI agents to provide assistance tailored to individual users. When a user looks for "the quiet restaurant we talked about before," for example, the model can help find saved information with a similar meaning, such as "a good place to talk," even if the restaurant's name is not entered. The model retrieves relevant information when needed, allowing the AI agent to generate responses based on the user's context. At if(kakao)26, Kakao also emphasized the role of embedding technology in connecting information from different parts of users' daily lives as a foundation for personalized AI agents.

In evaluations against similarly sized open embedding models, llama-nemotron-embed-1b-v2 and Qwen3-Embedding-4B, the two models achieved the best performance on Korean-language tasks and comparable performance on English-language tasks, and showed higher inference efficiency than Qwen3-Embedding. Kakao also confirmed better search performance than its earlier Kanana embedding series, along with memory efficiency and inference speed improvements of dozens of times or more.

...

The models can also be optimized for efficiency in different deployment environments. Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) lets developers adjust the number of values used in an embedding vector, the set of numbers that expresses the meaning of text, so developers can choose a vector size that balances search performance, storage requirements and processing speed.

Both models are released under the Kanana Open License, which allows research and development as well as commercial use, subject to its terms. Researchers and companies in Korea and abroad can evaluate the released models themselves and use them to build personalized AI agents and semantic search services.

signals.excerpt:
TorchTPU is an open-source project developed by Google in collaboration with Meta that provides a native PyTorch backend for Google TPUs. It enables PyTorch workloads to execute on TPU hardware with minimal code modifications, supporting eager and compiled execution, distributed computing, and hardware-specific optimizations.

...

Specifically, migrating from GPUs to TPUs involves replacing the `cuda` device with `tpu` and the `nccl` distributed backend with `tpu_dist`. Alternatively, developers can use the new `torch.accelerator.current_accelerator` API to identify the available accelerator, as shown in the following snippet.

...

TorchTPU support three eager execution modes: strict, debug, and DeferAndFuse. The latter is a new hybrid eager/compiled execution mode that Google claims "can be 50% or more faster than Strict Eager while reducing peak HBM memory".

To test TorchTPU's ability to run existing PyTorch models with no modifications, Google built an integration pipeline to evaluate about 5,000 Hugging Face models across 500+ architectures in both eager and compiled modes on TPU hardware generations starting from v5e.

...

To validate TorchTPU's performance, Google ran a 30-billion parameter Muse Glimmer model implemented in standard PyTorch. On a single TPUv7 chip, inference throughput reached 25.7k token/s at 5120 sequence length and 22.4k token/s at 10,240 sequence length. For training, using four TPUv7 chips, throughput reached 5.6k token/s and 4.6k token/s at 5120 and 10,240 sequence length, respectively.

...

TorchTPU is still at an early stage and therefore in continuous evolution. The project's roadmap include work on dynamic shapes, compilation performance, operator coverage, reinforcement learning, and quantization. For further details, make sure to read the original announcement, which provides a more comprehensive view of TorchTPU's architecture and scope.
